title: Conjugal Visits: Not exactly what you think
summary: Josh and Chuck examine conjugal visits and extended family visits in U.S. prisons. They trace the origins to Parchment Farm, a for-profit Mississippi labor camp where a warden began bringing in sex workers for inmates around 1918 as a work incentive, with a racist basis. The program was later extended to white inmates, then to women, and by the 1960s became framed as family rehabilitation. The hosts describe how extended family visits work today (apartment-style units, home-cooked meals, searches, eligibility rules, health screening), note that only a handful of states still allow them, and survey international practice. They cover the arguments against (cost, morality, security, punishment) and the data supporting visits (recidivism reductions, sexual assault findings), and discuss COVID-era shifts to virtual visits. The episode closes with a listener mail about Dirty Dancing and Frances Perkins.

segments.title: Opening and setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the conjugal visits topic, note that it is poorly understood, and frame the discussion around extended family visits and the decline of these programs in the US.

segments.title: Origins at Parchment Farm
segments.summary: Parchment Farm, a for-profit Mississippi labor camp, started bringing in sex workers for inmates around 1918 as a work incentive, based on racist assumptions. The program was extended to white inmates twelve years later and to women about fifty-four years later, in 1972. A 1966 study called it enlightened, and by 1963 the program was limited to spouses.

segments.title: Spread across states and the tough-on-crime shift
segments.summary: Extended visitation spread across states in the 1960s, peaking in the early 1990s with seventeen states. The decline followed the shift away from rehabilitation in the 1980s and 1990s toward tougher punishment.

segments.title: Evolution into extended family visits
segments.summary: Conjugal visits evolved into extended family visits or family reunion visits, involving children, parents and siblings rather than only sex. The purposes are incentive for good behavior and maintaining family ties to ease reentry after release.

segments.title: How visits work today
segments.summary: Visits happen at state prisons and vary by facility. Connecticut's McDougall Walker unit has a two-bedroom apartment where families can cook home-cooked meals. Visits last one to four days, with guard searches, fees in some states, and health and STD screening. Eligibility requires good behavior, prior visitor history, and participation in school or work programs. Serious violent or child-related offenses disqualify inmates. Federal prisons generally do not offer these visits.

segments.title: International comparisons
segments.summary: Only seven US states still allow these visits, down from seventeen. Japan, New Zealand, Ireland, and the UK generally do not. Countries including India, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Canada, Germany, Russia, Spain, France, Mexico, and Israel allow conjugal or family visits in some form, with variations. The Germany case involved an inmate who killed his girlfriend during a visit, which led to tighter restrictions rather than abolition.

segments.title: Arguments against and the data
segments.summary: The hosts review arguments against visits: cost, morality, security, and punishment. They argue these rest on gut reactions, not data. New Mexico's Michael Guzman case is cited as the main example against. Data cited includes a sixty-seven percent reduction in recidivism with such programs, a Minnesota study, and a 2011 finding that regular visits reduce return to prison. A study also linked family visitation to lower inmate sexual assault rates.

segments.title: Family bonds, COVID, and closing reflections
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why extended visits allow hard conversations, the statistics on children with incarcerated parents, and how COVID-era virtual visits may become a cheaper substitute. They encourage listeners in prisons or with family visit experiences to write in.

segments.title: Listener mail: Dirty Dancing and Frances Perkins
segments.summary: A listener notes that the character Baby in Dirty Dancing is named after Frances Perkins, the first woman in the cabinet, as she says in the movie.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and close the episode, inviting mail to the show address.
